inoculation with effective rhizobia can be expected to be successful in most situations, and that environmental factors are not likely to be important in controlling the outcome of inoculation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

inoculum performance was not affected by environmental variables in a predictable way, and that the size of the resident rhizobia population was the major variable affecting nodule occupancy by the inoculant.
the success of inoculant strains was highly variable, and that the success of any given strain depended on both environmental variables and the strain.
environmental variables had little effect on the outcome of competition between inoculated and indigenous strains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the competitive success of inoculant rhizobia can be predicted by the number of native rhizobia present.
the size of the resident rhizobial community is a major factor controlling the success of inoculant strains.
inoculants are most likely to be successful when they contain a high proportion of the dominant indigenous rhizobium, and when the indigenous rhizobia population is relatively low in numbers.
